name: Learn: Build, Commit, OCI, Save & Push Images
objective: CKAD › Application Design and Build (20%) + supply chain. The full image lifecycle: build from a Dockerfile, snapshot a running container with commit, modify/tag, save to a .tgz, export to the OCI format, load into the cluster and run it, and push to a registry.
description: Seven practicals across the whole image toolchain — Dockerfile build, docker commit, OCI-format export, save/load, and registry push — graded against your host Docker + the kindlab cluster.

questions.title: Build an image from a Dockerfile
questions.teach:
Build an image from a **Dockerfile** plus a **build context** (the directory you hand the builder): `docker build -t name:tag <context>`. The `-t` names and tags the result in one shot.

**Gotcha:** the context path is positional, not the Dockerfile path — `.` means the current dir, not the Dockerfile's dir. Skip `-t` and you get a dangling `<none>:<none>` image.
questions.prompt:
A build context is prepared at `/tmp/kindlab-img` (a `Dockerfile` + `hello.txt`). Build an image tagged `myapp:1.0` from it.

Target: `docker image inspect myapp:1.0` succeeds and the image carries the Dockerfile's `LABEL stage=base`.
questions.hint: `docker build -t myapp:1.0 /tmp/kindlab-img` — then `docker image inspect myapp:1.0` to confirm it exists.
questions.solution:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 /tmp/kindlab-img
docker image inspect myapp:1.0 --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "stage" }}'   # base

verification.description: image myapp:1.0 built from the provided Dockerfile

questions.title: Commit a running container into an image
questions.teach:
`docker commit <container> name:tag` snapshots a running container's current filesystem into a new image — a quick way to capture ad-hoc state without a Dockerfile.

**Gotcha:** commit captures only the container's writable layer; it does **not** include mounted volumes, and the result keeps the base image's `CMD`/`ENV` unless you override them with `--change`.
questions.prompt:
A container named `appbox` (busybox) is already running. Snapshot its current state into an image named `committed:1.0` using `docker commit`.

Target: `docker image inspect committed:1.0` succeeds.
questions.hint: `docker commit appbox committed:1.0`, then `docker image inspect committed:1.0`.
questions.solution:
docker commit appbox committed:1.0
docker image inspect committed:1.0 --format '{{.Id}}'

verification.description: running container 'appbox' committed to image committed:1.0

questions.title: Modify the image: add a label and tag
questions.teach:
You can stamp a label onto an image at build time without touching the Dockerfile: `docker build -t myapp:2.0 --label version=2 <context>`. It lands under `.Config.Labels`, the same place a Dockerfile `LABEL` would.

**Gotcha:** `--label` writes config metadata, not a new filesystem layer — verify with `docker image inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "version" }}'`, not `docker history`.
questions.prompt:
Rebuild the same context as `myapp:2.0`, adding an image label `version=2` **via the build flag** (don't edit the Dockerfile).

Target: image `myapp:2.0` exists and its config label `version` equals `2`.
questions.hint: `docker build -t myapp:2.0 --label version=2 /tmp/kindlab-img`. Verify: `docker image inspect myapp:2.0 --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "version" }}'`.
questions.solution:
docker build -t myapp:2.0 --label version=2 /tmp/kindlab-img
docker image inspect myapp:2.0 --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "version" }}'   # 2

verification.description: image myapp:2.0 built with label version=2

questions.title: Save the image to a .tgz tarball
questions.teach:
`docker save name:tag` writes an image (all layers + metadata) to a tarball so it can move between machines without a registry; reload it with `docker load -i`. The archive holds a `manifest.json`.

**Gotcha:** `docker save` produces an **uncompressed** tar — pipe through `gzip` to get a genuine `.tgz`. Just renaming a plain tar to `.tgz` does not compress it.
questions.prompt:
Save the `myapp:2.0` image to a gzipped tarball at `/tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-2.0.tgz`.

Target: the file exists and is a valid docker image archive (contains `manifest.json`).
questions.hint: `docker save myapp:2.0 | gzip > /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-2.0.tgz`. Check it: `tar -tzf /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-2.0.tgz | grep manifest.json`.
questions.solution:
docker save myapp:2.0 | gzip > /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-2.0.tgz
tar -tzf /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-2.0.tgz | grep manifest.json   # present

verification.description: myapp:2.0 saved to a valid gzipped Docker image archive

questions.title: Export to the OCI image format
questions.teach:
The vendor-neutral **OCI image layout** is the open-standard archive format, recognised by an `oci-layout` marker plus `index.json`. Build straight to it with `docker buildx build --output type=oci,dest=out.tar <context>`.

**Gotcha:** `docker save` writes the **Docker** format (`manifest.json`), **not** OCI — a common trap when a task says 'OCI'. Use buildx (or skopeo) instead.
questions.prompt:
Export the build context at `/tmp/kindlab-img` to an **OCI-format** archive at `/tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-oci.tar` using buildx.

Target: the archive is a valid OCI image layout (contains `oci-layout` and `index.json`).
questions.hint: `docker buildx build --output type=oci,dest=/tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-oci.tar /tmp/kindlab-img`. Verify: `tar -tf /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-oci.tar | grep -E 'oci-layout|index.json'` (NOT `docker save`, which is Docker format).
questions.solution:
docker buildx build --output type=oci,dest=/tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-oci.tar /tmp/kindlab-img
tar -tf /tmp/kindlab-img/myapp-oci.tar | grep -E 'oci-layout|index.json'   # both present

verification.description: myapp-oci.tar is a valid OCI image layout (oci-layout + index.json)

questions.title: Load the image into the cluster and run it
questions.teach:
kind nodes run their own containerd image store, separate from host Docker, so a locally-built image is invisible to the cluster until you copy it in: `kind load docker-image name:tag --name <cluster>`. Then run the pod with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` so the kubelet uses the on-node copy.

**Gotcha:** `kind load` must target the right `--name`; a missing or mis-named load shows up as `ErrImagePull`/`ImagePullBackOff` on the pod.
questions.prompt:
Make `myapp:2.0` available to the `kindlab` cluster, then in namespace `images-learn` run a pod named `myapp` using it, with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`.

Target: pod `myapp` in `images-learn` is `Running` using image `myapp:2.0`.
questions.hint: `kind load docker-image myapp:2.0 --name kindlab`, then `kubectl -n images-learn run myapp --image=myapp:2.0 --image-pull-policy=IfNotPresent`.
questions.solution:
kind load docker-image myapp:2.0 --name kindlab
kubectl -n images-learn run myapp --image=myapp:2.0 --image-pull-policy=IfNotPresent
kubectl -n images-learn get pod myapp -o wide

verification.description: pod myapp is Running from the local image myapp:2.0

questions.title: Push the image to a registry
questions.teach:
To push to a registry you first retag the image so its name embeds the registry host, then push: `docker tag myapp:2.0 localhost:5001/myapp:2.0` then `docker push localhost:5001/myapp:2.0`. Check it landed via the HTTP API: `GET /v2/_catalog`.

**Gotcha:** the registry host must be in the image name — a bare `docker push myapp:2.0` goes to Docker Hub, not your local registry.
questions.prompt:
A local registry runs at `localhost:5001`. Tag `myapp:2.0` as `localhost:5001/myapp:2.0` and push it.

Target: the registry's catalog lists repo `myapp` with tag `2.0`.
questions.hint: `docker tag myapp:2.0 localhost:5001/myapp:2.0` then `docker push localhost:5001/myapp:2.0`. Confirm: `curl -s localhost:5001/v2/_catalog` and `curl -s localhost:5001/v2/myapp/tags/list`.

verification.description: myapp:2.0 pushed to the local registry (catalog + tag)
